title: Why should you first clarify what "1 million users" means (registered vs daily-active vs concurrent) before designing, since the real driver is requests/sec, read/write ratio, data size, and latency/consistency requirements?
shortTitle: Why should you first clarify what "1 million users" means
keyPoints: One million users is a marketing number, not an engineering one: registered, daily-active, and concurrent differ by orders of magnitude
The real engineering driver is peak requests per second, derived from daily-active users with a peak-to-average multiplier
The read-to-write ratio shapes the entire data strategy: read-heavy benefits from caching, write-heavy needs sharding
Data size and growth rate drive storage and partitioning decisions
Latency and consistency requirements are the decisive drivers: a bank balance demands strong consistency
These four drivers, not the user count, determine capacity, data architecture, and the consistency model
Always derive these numbers before designing to avoid over-engineering or under-provisioning

s1_definition.oneliner: One million users is a marketing number, not an engineering one: you must convert it into peak requests per second, read-to-write ratio, data size, and latency and consistency targets before you can design anything.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Registered users** – everyone who ever signed up; most are dormant and irrelevant to capacity.
- **Daily-active users (DAU)** – those who actually use the system in a day; the basis for request estimation.
- **Concurrent users** – those active at the same instant; what hardware must survive at peak.
- **Peak requests per second** – derived from DAU, per-user request rate, and a peak-to-average multiplier.
- **Read-to-write ratio** – shapes the data strategy: caching for reads, sharding for writes.
- **Data size and growth** – determines whether a single database suffices or sharding is needed.
- **Latency and consistency** – tight latency forces caching; strong consistency constrains distribution.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine someone tells National Bank of India "we have a million customers, build a branch big enough." That tells you almost nothing about how many counters to build. A million customers on the books might mean only fifty thousand visit in a day, and of those maybe two thousand are inside at the busiest moment on salary day. If you built for a million at once, you waste a fortune. If you built for the average and ignored salary-day rush, the branch overflows. So before pouring any concrete, a good architect asks: how many are actually inside at peak, how many just read their balance versus make a transaction, how much paperwork do we store, and how fast must each customer be served?

  │        Clarify the Number             │
  │                                       │
  │  Registered:    1,000,000 (irrelevant)│

  │      Derive the Four Drivers          │
  │                                       │

  │  3. Data Growth:     67 GB/year       │

sections.s6_takeaway:
Before designing anything for scale, always clarify what a number like one million users actually means. Registered users, daily-active users, and concurrent users can differ by orders of magnitude. A million registered users might be only a hundred thousand daily-active and a few thousand concurrent at peak. Designing for the wrong one is the classic mistake that leads either to a wildly expensive over-build or to an outage on the first busy day.

The real work is converting that headline into four derived drivers: peak requests per second, derived from DAU and a peak-to-average multiplier; the read-to-write ratio, which shapes the entire data strategy; data size and growth rate, which determines partitioning needs; and latency and consistency requirements, which are often the decisive constraints. At National Bank of India, a product manager said "build for one million users," and the first instinct was to treat that as a million concurrent. Once we clarified it into about a hundred thousand DAU and a few thousand concurrent at peak, the right design was dramatically simpler.

These four drivers, not the user count, determine capacity, data architecture, and the consistency model. A 97.8% read-heavy workload with strong consistency on balances leads to a very different architecture than a write-heavy trading platform with eventual consistency.

Remember one sentence: one million users is the start of the conversation, not the answer: the real work is converting it into peak requests per second, read-to-write ratio, data size, and latency and consistency requirements.
